title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 2, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 22–23 (Night 231, continuing nights-230; the opening of the night, with its formula, stood on printed pp. 20–21, which are missing from the only scan of volume 2, so the text begins mid-sentence), transcribed from the scan (archive.org aliflailaorbook02unkngoog) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 231 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. Its opening is lost from the only surviving scan of the second volume, and the text takes up with al-Amjad waiting in a lane with the young woman he met in the city, before a house he has let her think is his. She breaks the lock with a stone and walks in; inside is a richly furnished hall, set out with food, fruit, wine and purses of gold, and al-Amjad, sure the owner will come and kill him, sits with her in terror while she eats, drinks and teases him. Then the master of the house arrives: Bahādur, a mamlūk of the king who serves as his master of the horse and keeps the hall for his own pleasures; and morning overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: وَنَحْنُ قَاعِدُونَ فِى الزُّقَاقِ
sentences.tr: wa-naḥnu qāʿidūna fī al-zuqāqi
sentences.l: […] and-we (are) sitting in the-lane.
sentences.i: […] while we sit waiting in the lane.
sentences.n: The beginning of this night is skipped here for now: it stood on pages missing from the only scan of this volume (printed pp. 20–21), and the text resumes mid-sentence. When it resumes, al-Amjad has evidently brought the young woman to the door of a house that is not his, pretending it is, and is putting her off as though waiting for a slave of his to come and open it. wa-naḥnu qāʿidūna, 'while we are sitting', is a circumstantial clause; the rest of the sentence is lost with the missing pages. فى is printed with a dotless ى for fī, as the edition often does; it is kept as set.
sentences.gap: Opening of Night 231 (before P932L01): not in the scan

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَامَتِ الصَّبِيَّةُ إِلَى الضَّبَّةِ بِحَجَرٍ
sentences.tr: thumma qāmati al-ṣabiyyatu ilā al-ḍabbati bi-ḥajarin
sentences.l: Then rose the-girl to the-lock with-a-stone.
sentences.i: Then the girl got up and went at the lock with a stone.
sentences.n: al-ḍabba: Lane gives an iron plate or clamp fastened on a door; in later usage it is the door-lock or bolt itself. Its shadda is printed. qāmat ilā, 'she rose (and went) to'. bi-ḥajarin: bi- of the instrument, 'with a stone'. The final -i of qāmati is only a helping vowel before the article.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا الْأَمْجَدُ لَا تَعْجَلِي وَاصْبِرِي حَتَّى يَجِيءَ الْمَمْلُوكُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā al-Amjadu lā taʿjalī wa-iṣbirī ḥattā yajīʾa al-mamlūku
sentences.l: And-said to-her al-Amjad: Do-not hurry, and-be-patient until comes the-slave.
sentences.i: Al-Amjad said to her, “Don't be hasty; wait until the slave comes.”
sentences.n: al-mamlūk, 'the slave', literally 'the owned one', a bought servant: the slave al-Amjad has apparently claimed is on his way with the key. ḥattā with the subjunctive, yajīʾa, 'until he comes'. The ء of يجيء is printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمْ تَسْمَعْ كَلَامَهُ بَلْ ضَرَبَتِ الضَّبَّةَ بِالْحَجَرِ فَقَسَمَتْهَا نِصْفَيْنِ فَانْفَتَحَ الْبَابُ
sentences.tr: fa-lam tasmaʿ kalāmahu bal ḍarabati al-ḍabbata bi-al-ḥajari fa-qasamathā niṣfayni fa-infataḥa al-bābu
sentences.l: But-she-did-not hear his-speech; rather she-struck the-lock with-the-stone and-split-it (into) two-halves, and-came-open the-door.
sentences.i: But she paid no heed to what he said: she struck the lock with the stone and split it in two, and the door swung open.
sentences.n: lam tasmaʿ kalāmahu, 'she did not hear his words': she would not listen. niṣfayni, 'two halves', dual accusative. infataḥa, Form VII of f-t-ḥ, 'to come open'.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا وَأَيُّ شَيْءٍ خَطَرَلَكِ حَتَّى تَفْعَلِي هٰكَذَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā wa-ayyu shayʾin khaṭara laki ḥattā tafʿalī hākadhā
sentences.l: And-he-said to-her: And-what thing occurred-to-you that you-do thus?
sentences.i: “What came into your head,” he asked her, “to make you do such a thing?”
sentences.n: khaṭara li-, 'to occur to, cross the mind of': li- marks the one in whose mind the thought arises. The print runs khaṭara laki together as خطرلكِ, with the kasra of -ki printed; it is kept as set. The shadda of ايّ and the ء of شيء are printed. ḥattā here means 'so that', of result. hākadhā is written defectively, هكذا, and takes a dagger alif.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ يُوهْ يُوهْ يَاسَيِّدِي وَإِيشْ جَرَي أَمَا هُوَ بَيْتُكَ وَمَوْضِعُكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu yūh yūh yā-sayyidī wa-īsh jarā amā huwa baytuka wa-mawḍiʿuka
sentences.l: And-she-said to-him: Yoh, yoh, O-my-lord, and-what happened? Is-it-not your-house and-your-place?
sentences.i: “Oh, come now, my lord!” she said. “What does it matter? Isn't it your own house, your own place?”
sentences.n: yūh, a colloquial exclamation of surprise or impatience, something like 'oh!' or 'come now!'. īsh, written ايش, is the colloquial contraction of ayyu shayʾin, 'what thing?', the common Middle Arabic 'what'; wa-īsh jarā, 'and what has happened?', that is, 'what of it?'. The print writes jarā with ي, جري, for the usual ى; kept as set. It also runs yā sayyidī together, ياسيدي, as it often does. amā, 'is it not…?', is interrogative a- with the negative mā; its fatḥa is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ نَعَمْ وَلٰكِنْ لَا يَحْتَاجُ إِلَى كَسْرِ الضَّبَّةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla naʿam wa-lākin lā yaḥtāju ilā kasri al-ḍabbati
sentences.l: And-he-said: Yes, but it-does-not need to breaking (of) the-lock.
sentences.i: “Yes,” he said, “but there was no need to break the lock.”
sentences.n: iḥtāja ilā, 'to need': the verb takes ilā for what is needed, and with no subject expressed it means 'there is no need for'. lākin is written defectively, لكن, and takes a dagger alif.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الصَّبِيَّةَ دَخَلَتِ الْبَيْتَ فَبَقِيَ الْأَمْجَدُ مُتَحَيِّرًا فِي نَفْسِهِ خَوْفًا مِنْ أَصْحَابِ الْمَنْزِلِ وَلَمْ يَدْرِ مَا ذَا يَصْنَعُ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-ṣabiyyata dakhalati al-bayta fa-baqiya al-Amjadu mutaḥayyiran fī nafsihi khawfan min aṣḥābi al-manzili wa-lam yadri mā dhā yaṣnaʿu
sentences.l: Then indeed the-girl entered the-house, and-remained al-Amjad bewildered in himself, (out of) fear of (the) owners (of) the-dwelling, and-he-did-not know what (is) that he-should-do.
sentences.i: Then the girl went into the house, and al-Amjad was left standing at a loss, afraid of the people the house belonged to, and not knowing what to do.
sentences.n: thumma inna, 'then (it was that)', a common narrative opener; inna puts its noun in the accusative, al-ṣabiyyata, whose shadda is printed here. baqiya, 'remained', with the circumstantial accusative mutaḥayyiran, 'bewildered'. khawfan min, an accusative of cause, 'out of fear of'. lam yadri is the jussive of darā, its final yāʾ dropped. The print sets mā dhā as two words; kept as set.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ الصَّبِيَّةُ لِمَ لَمْ تَدْخُلْ يَانُورَ عَيْنِي وَحُشَاشَةَ قَلْبِي
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu al-ṣabiyyatu lima lam tadkhul yā-nūra ʿaynī wa-ḥushāshata qalbī
sentences.l: And-said to-him the-girl: Why did-you-not enter, O-light (of) my-eye and-last-breath (of) my-heart?
sentences.i: “Why don't you come in,” the girl said to him, “light of my eyes, life of my heart?”
sentences.n: lima, 'why?', is li- + mā shortened; its vowels are printed. ḥushāsha is the last remnant of life or spirit left in one (Lane), so ḥushāshat qalbī is 'the very life of my heart', an endearment. The print runs yā nūra together, يانور; kept as set.

sentences.t: قَالَ لَهَا سَمْعًا وَطَاعَةً وَلٰكِنْ قَدْ أَبْطَأَ عَلَيَّ الْمَمْلُوكُ
sentences.tr: qāla lahā samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan wa-lākin qad abṭaʾa ʿalayya al-mamlūku
sentences.l: He-said to-her: (With) hearing and-obedience; but indeed has-been-slow upon-me the-slave.
sentences.i: He said to her, “With hearing and obedience; but my slave is slow in coming.”
sentences.n: samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan, 'with hearing and obedience': two accusatives standing for a whole sentence of assent. abṭaʾa ʿalā, 'to be slow in coming to (someone)': ʿalā marks the one kept waiting. The shadda of عليّ and the ء of ابطأ are printed.

sentences.t: وَمَا أَدْرِي هَلْ فَعَلَ شَيْأً مِمَّا قُلْتُ لَهُ عَلَيْهِ وَأَمَرْتُهُ بِهِ أَمْ لَاثُمَّ إِنَّهُ دَخَلَ مَعَهَا وَهُوَ فِي غَايَةِ مَايَكُونُ مِنَ الْخَوْفِ مِنْ أَصْحَابِ الْمَنْزِلِ
sentences.tr: wa-mā adrī hal faʿala shayʾan mimmā qultu lahu ʿalayhi wa-amartuhu bihi am lā thumma innahu dakhala maʿahā wa-huwa fī ghāyati mā yakūnu mina al-khawfi min aṣḥābi al-manzili
sentences.l: And-not I-know whether he-did a-thing of-what I-told him about-it and-ordered-him with-it or not. Then indeed-he entered with-her, and-he (was) in (the) utmost (of) what may-be of the-fear of (the) owners (of) the-dwelling.
sentences.i: “And I don't know whether he has done any of what I told him and bade him do, or not.” Then he went in with her, as frightened of the owners of the house as a man can be.
sentences.n: shayʾan is printed شيأ, with the hamza on an alif seat and no final alif for the tanwīn; kept as set. mimmā is min + mā, 'of what'. qultu lahu ʿalayhi, 'I told him about it', sits oddly beside amartuhu bihi, 'I ordered him (to do) it' (amara takes bi- for the thing ordered); the ʿalayhi may be a slip or a loose colloquial qāla ʿalā, 'to speak of'. It is read as printed. The print runs lā and thumma together, لاثم, so this unit runs on across the sentence break. fī ghāyati mā yakūnu mina al-khawf, 'in the utmost there can be of fear', is also printed run together, مايكون. wa-huwa … is a circumstantial clause, 'while he was …'.

sentences.t: وَلَمَّا دَخَلَ الْبَيْتَ وَجَدَ فِيهِ قَاعَةً مَلِيحَةً بِأَرْبَعَةِ لَوَاوِينَ مُتَقَابِلَةٍ وَفِيهَا خَزَائِنُ وَسَدَّلَاتٌ مَفْرُوشَاتٌ بِالْفُرُشِ الْحَرِيرِ وَالدِّيبَاجِ
sentences.tr: wa-lammā dakhala al-bayta wajada fīhi qāʿatan malīḥatan bi-arbaʿati lawāwīna mutaqābilatin wa-fīhā khazāʾinu wa-saddalātun mafrūshātun bi-al-furushi al-ḥarīri wa-al-dībāji
sentences.l: And-when he-entered the-house he-found in-it a-hall fine with-four līwāns facing-one-another, and-in-it cupboards and-couches spread with-the-coverings, the-silk and-the-brocade.
sentences.i: When he went in, he found inside a handsome hall with four raised alcoves facing one another; in it were cupboards and couches spread with coverings of silk and brocade.
sentences.n: qāʿa, the hall or great reception room of a town house. lawāwīn is the spoken plural of līwān (book Arabic īwān, pl. ayāwīn), a raised alcove opening onto the hall; four of them facing one another make the classic cross-shaped hall. bi-arbaʿati: bi- 'with', of what the hall has. The ئ of خزائن, 'cupboards', is printed. سدّلات is uncertain: it seems to be the plural of a later word, sidilla, a couch, bench or raised seat along the wall, probably of Persian origin; it is vocalised here by the print's own shadda on the dāl, saddalāt, with doubt. mafrūshāt bi-, 'spread with': bi- names the covering. al-furush al-ḥarīr, 'the coverings, the silk': the material is set beside the noun in apposition, a common loose construction.

sentences.t: وَفِي وَسَطِ الْقَاعَةِ فِسْقِيَّهٌ مُثَمَّنَةٌ مَرْصُوصٌ عَلَيْهَا أَطْبَاقٌ مُرَصَّعَةٌ بِفُصُوصِ الْجَوَاهِرِ وَهِيَ مَمْلُوءَةٌ فَاكِهَةً وَمَشْمُومًا
sentences.tr: wa-fī wasaṭi al-qāʿati fisqiyyatun muthammanatun marṣūṣun ʿalayhā aṭbāqun muraṣṣaʿatun bi-fuṣūṣi al-jawāhiri wa-hiya mamlūʾatun fākihatan wa-mashmūman
sentences.l: And-in (the) middle (of) the-hall a-fountain-basin eight-sided, set-in-rows upon-it dishes studded with-stones (of) the-jewels, and-they (were) filled (with) fruit and-sweet-scents.
sentences.i: In the middle of the hall was an eight-sided fountain basin, with dishes set in rows upon it, studded with gemstones and heaped with fruit and fragrant flowers.
sentences.n: fisqiyya, a fountain basin or ornamental pool, a word of foreign and uncertain origin; the print writes it with ه for ة, as it often does, kept as set. muthammana, 'made eight-sided'. marṣūṣun ʿalayhā aṭbāqun, 'set in rows upon it (are) dishes': the participle comes first and stays in the masculine. fuṣūṣ, plural of faṣṣ, the stone set in a ring: 'studded with gems'. mamlūʾa, 'filled' (its ء is printed), takes accusatives of what fills them, fākihatan wa-mashmūman. mashmūm, literally 'something smelled', means scented flowers and herbs.

sentences.t: وَفِي جَانِبِهَا أَوَانِى الشَّرَابِ وَهُنَاكَ شَمْعَدَانٌ فِيهِ شَمْعَةٌ مُرَكَّبَةٌ
sentences.tr: wa-fī jānibihā awānī al-sharābi wa-hunāka shamʿadānun fīhi shamʿatun murakkabatun
sentences.l: And-in its-side (the) vessels (of) the-drink, and-there a-candlestick in-it a-candle fitted.
sentences.i: Beside it stood the wine vessels, and there was a candlestick with a candle set in it.
sentences.n: awānī is the plural of āniya, itself a plural of ināʾ, 'vessel'; the print spells it with ى, اوانى, kept as set. sharāb, 'drink', in scenes like this means wine. shamʿadān, 'candlestick', is from Persian. murakkaba, 'fitted, mounted', set in its socket.

sentences.t: وَالْمَكَانُ مَلْآنُ بِنَفِيسِ الْقُمَاشِ وَفِيهِ صَنَادِيقُ وَكَرَاسِيُّ مَنْصُوبَةٌ وَعَلَى كُلِّ كُرْسِيٍّ بُقْجَةٌ وَفَوْقَهَا كِيسٌ مَلْآنُ دَرَاهِمَ وَذَهَبٍ وَدَنَانِيرَ
sentences.tr: wa-al-makānu malʾānu bi-nafīsi al-qumāshi wa-fīhi ṣanādīqu wa-karāsiyyu manṣūbatun wa-ʿalā kulli kursiyyin buqjatun wa-fawqahā kīsun malʾānu darāhima wa-dhahabin wa-danānīra
sentences.l: And-the-place (was) full with-(the)-precious (of) the-fabric, and-in-it chests and-chairs set-up, and-on every chair a-bundle, and-above-it a-purse full (of) dirhams and-gold and-dinars.
sentences.i: The place was full of costly fabrics; there were chests in it, and chairs set out, and on every chair a bundle, and on each bundle a purse full of dirhams, gold and dinars.
sentences.n: The print has دارهم, a misprint for دراهم, corrected here. darāhim, 'dirhams', are silver coins; danānīr, 'dinars', gold ones. malʾān, 'full' (its madda is printed), takes bi- for what fills it in the first phrase, bi-nafīsi al-qumāsh, 'with the costly of fabric'; in the second it is annexed directly to what fills it, malʾānu darāhima wa-dhahabin wa-danānīra (darāhim and danānīr are diptotes, so their genitive ends in -a). The shadda of كرسيّ, 'chair', is printed. buqja, a cloth bundle for clothes, is from Turkish bohça.

sentences.t: وَالدَّارُ تَشْهَدُ لِصَاحِبِهَا بِالسَّعَادَةِ لِأَنَّ أَرْضَهَا مَفْرُوشَةٌ بِالرُّخَامِ
sentences.tr: wa-al-dāru tashhadu li-ṣāḥibihā bi-al-saʿādati li-anna arḍahā mafrūshatun bi-al-rukhāmi
sentences.l: And-the-house bears-witness for-its-owner to-the-prosperity, because its-floor (is) spread with-the-marble.
sentences.i: The house bore witness to its owner's good fortune, for its floor was paved with marble.
sentences.n: shahida li-… bi-…, 'to testify for (someone) to (something)': li- marks the one the testimony favours, bi- what it attests. saʿāda, 'good fortune, prosperity'. arḍ, 'ground', is here the floor.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَى الْأَمْجَدُ ذٰلِكَ تَحَيَّرَ فِي أَمْرِهِ وَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ قَدْ رَاحَتْ رُوحِي إِنَّا لِلّٰهِ وَإِنَّا إِلَيْهِ رَاجِعُونَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾā al-Amjadu dhālika taḥayyara fī amrihi wa-qāla fī nafsihi qad rāḥat rūḥī innā li-llāhi wa-innā ilayhi rājiʿūna
sentences.l: And-when saw al-Amjad that, he-was-bewildered in his-affair, and-said in himself: Indeed has-gone my-soul! Indeed-we (are) God's, and-indeed-we to-Him (are) returning.
sentences.i: When al-Amjad saw all this he was at his wits' end, and said to himself, “My life is as good as gone! To God we belong, and to Him we return.”
sentences.n: The print has امرة, a misprint for امره, corrected here. taḥayyara fī amrihi, 'he was perplexed in his affair', did not know what to do; the shadda of تحيّر is printed. rāḥat rūḥī, 'my soul has gone', that is, 'I am a dead man'. innā li-llāhi wa-innā ilayhi rājiʿūn is Qurʾān 2:156, said in the face of calamity; li- is of belonging, 'we are God's'. The shaddas of انّا are printed; ذلك and لله take a dagger alif.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا الصَّبِيَّةُ فَإِنَّهَا لَمَّا رَأَتْ ذٰلِكَ الْمَكَانَ فَرِحَتْ فَرَحًا شَدِيدًا مَا عَلَيْهِ مِنْ مَزِيدٍ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā al-ṣabiyyatu fa-innahā lammā raʾat dhālika al-makāna fariḥat faraḥan shadīdan mā ʿalayhi min mazīdin
sentences.l: And-as-for the-girl, indeed-she, when she-saw that place, rejoiced (with) a-rejoicing intense, not upon-it of increase.
sentences.i: As for the girl, when she saw the place she was overjoyed, with a joy that could not have been greater.
sentences.n: ammā … fa-, 'as for …': the topic, answered by fa-. The print writes raʾat as رات, with no seat for the hamza; kept as set. faraḥan shadīdan is a cognate accusative, 'rejoiced a great rejoicing'. mā ʿalayhi min mazīd, 'there is no increase upon it', is a stock phrase: as great as can be.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ وَاللّٰهِ يَا سَيِّدِي مَا قَصَّرَ مَمْلُوكُكَ فَإِنَّهُ مَسَحَ الْمَكَانَ وَطَبَخَ الطَّعَامَ وَهَيَّأَ الْفَاكِهَةَ وَقَدْ جِئْتُ أَنَا فِي أَحْسَنِ الْأَوْقَاتِ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat wa-allāhi yā sayyidī mā qaṣṣara mamlūkuka fa-innahu masaḥa al-makāna wa-ṭabakha al-ṭaʿāma wa-hayyaʾa al-fākihata wa-qad jiʾtu anā fī aḥsani al-awqāti
sentences.l: And-she-said: By-God, O my-lord, not fell-short your-slave; for-he wiped the-place and-cooked the-food and-prepared the-fruit, and-indeed came I at (the) best (of) the-times.
sentences.i: “By God, my lord,” she said, “your slave has not been remiss: he has cleaned the place, cooked the food and set out the fruit, and I have come at just the right time.”
sentences.n: She takes all this for the work of al-Amjad's slave. wa-allāhi: wa- of the oath, 'by God'. qaṣṣara, Form II, 'to fall short, neglect a duty'. masaḥa, 'to wipe', here 'cleaned'. The shadda and ء of هيّأ and the damma of جئتُ are printed. jiʾtu anā: the pronoun adds weight, 'I myself have come'.

sentences.t: فَلَمْ يَلْتَفِتْ إِلَيْهَا الْأَمْجَدُ لِاشْتِغَالِ قَلْبِهِ بِالْخَوْفِ مِنْ أَصْحَابِ الْمَكَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-lam yaltafit ilayhā al-Amjadu li-ishtighāli qalbihi bi-al-khawfi min aṣḥābi al-makāni
sentences.l: But-did-not turn to-her al-Amjad, for-(the)-preoccupation (of) his-heart with-the-fear of (the) owners (of) the-place.
sentences.i: But al-Amjad paid her no attention, his heart being wholly taken up with fear of the owners of the place.
sentences.n: iltafata ilā, 'to turn towards, pay attention to'. li-ishtighāli: li- of cause, 'because of the preoccupation of'; ishtaghala bi-, 'to be occupied with', so bi- names what fills his heart.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ يُوهْ يَا سَيِّدِي يَا كَبِدِي مَالَكَ وَاقِفًا هٰكَذَا
sentences.tr: fa-qālat yūh yā sayyidī yā kabidī mā laka wāqifan hākadhā
sentences.l: And-she-said: Yoh, O my-lord, O my-liver, what (is) to-you standing thus?
sentences.i: “Oh, my lord, my darling,” she said, “why are you standing there like that?”
sentences.n: yā kabidī, 'O my liver': the liver, like the heart, is a seat of tender feeling, so 'my darling'. mā laka, 'what is with you?', is printed as one word, مالك; li- marks the one concerned, and wāqifan, 'standing', is a circumstantial accusative: 'what ails you, standing so?'

sentences.t: ثُمَّ شَهَقَتْ شَهْقَةً وَأَعْطَتِ الْأَمْجَدَ قُبْلَةً مِثْلَ كَسْرِ الْجَوْزِ
sentences.tr: thumma shahaqat shahqatan wa-aʿṭati al-Amjada qublatan mithla kasri al-jawzi
sentences.l: Then she-gasped a-gasp and-gave al-Amjad a-kiss like (the) cracking (of) the-walnuts.
sentences.i: Then she gave a little gasp and planted a kiss on al-Amjad that cracked like a breaking walnut.
sentences.n: shahaqat shahqatan, a cognate accusative, 'she drew in her breath sharply'. qublatan mithla kasri al-jawz, 'a kiss like the cracking of walnuts': a loud, smacking kiss.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ لَهُ يَا سَيِّدِي إِنْ كُنْتَ مُوَاعِدَ غَيْرِي فَأَنَا أَشُدُّ ظَهْرِي وَأَخْدُمُهَا
sentences.tr: wa-qālat lahu yā sayyidī in kunta muwāʿida ghayrī fa-anā ashuddu ẓahrī wa-akhdumuhā
sentences.l: And-she-said to-him: O my-lord, if you-were having-a-tryst-with other-than-me, then-I tighten my-back and-serve-her.
sentences.i: “My lord,” she said to him, “if you have arranged to meet another woman, I will gird myself and wait on her.”
sentences.n: muwāʿid is the active participle of wāʿada, 'to make an appointment with'; here it is annexed to its object, muwāʿida ghayrī, 'one who has a tryst with someone other than me'. shadda ẓahrahu, 'to tighten (the belt round) one's back', is to gird oneself for work; the shadda of اشدّ is printed. akhdumuhā, 'I will serve her': the -hā assumes the rival is a woman. She is teasing him, taking his gloom for fear that another lover is due.

sentences.t: فَضَحِكَ الْأَمْجَدُ مِنْ قَلْبٍ مَمْلُوهٍ بِالْغَيْظِ
sentences.tr: fa-ḍaḥika al-Amjadu min qalbin mamlūʾin bi-al-ghayẓi
sentences.l: And-laughed al-Amjad from a-heart filled with-the-rage.
sentences.i: Al-Amjad laughed, from a heart full of vexation.
sentences.n: mamlūʾ, 'filled', is printed مملوه, with ه where the hamza should stand (compare مملوءة above); kept as set and read mamlūʾ. ghayẓ is rage or bitter vexation: he laughs because he must.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ طَلَعَ وَجَلَسَ وَهُوَ يَنْفُخُ وَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ يَا قَتْلَةَ الشُّومِ إِذَا جَاءَ صَاحِبُ الْمَنْزِلِ
sentences.tr: thumma ṭalaʿa wa-jalasa wa-huwa yanfukhu wa-qāla fī nafsihi yā qatlata al-shūmi idhā jāʾa ṣāḥibu al-manzili
sentences.l: Then he-went-up and-sat, and-he (was) puffing, and-he-said in himself: O killing (of) the-ill-luck, when comes (the) owner (of) the-dwelling!
sentences.i: Then he went up and sat down, breathing hard, and said to himself, “What an ill-starred death I shall die when the master of the house comes!”
sentences.n: ṭalaʿa, 'he went up', presumably onto one of the raised līwāns. yanfukhu, 'blowing, puffing', with anxiety. yā qatlata al-shūm, 'O killing of ill luck!', is a colloquial cry of foreboding: qatla is 'a killing', and shūm is the spoken form of shuʾm, 'ill luck', its hamza softened; the yā is a cry of lament, not an address to anyone. idhā jāʾa, 'when (he) comes': the perfect after idhā refers to the future. The ء of جاء is printed.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ جَلَسَتِ الصَّبِيَّةُ إِلَى جَانِبِهِ وَصَارَتْ تَلْعَبُ وَتَضْحَكُ وَالْأَمْجَدُ مَهْمُومٌ مُعَبِّسٌ يَحْسِبُ فِي نَفْسِهِ أَلْفَ حِسَابٍ
sentences.tr: wa-qad jalasati al-ṣabiyyatu ilā jānibihi wa-ṣārat talʿabu wa-taḍḥaku wa-al-Amjadu mahmūmun muʿabbisun yaḥsibu fī nafsihi alfa ḥisābin
sentences.l: And-had sat the-girl at his-side, and-she-became playing and-laughing, while-al-Amjad (was) troubled, frowning, reckoning in himself a-thousand reckonings.
sentences.i: The girl had sat down beside him and set about playing and laughing, while al-Amjad sat troubled and scowling, turning over a thousand calculations in his mind.
sentences.n: ṣārat talʿabu, 'she became playing': ṣāra with an imperfect means 'began to, set about', a construction the Nights uses constantly. muʿabbis, 'frowning', is a Form II participle; its shadda is printed. yaḥsibu … alfa ḥisābin, 'reckoning a thousand reckonings': weighing every possibility.

sentences.t: وَيَقُولُ لَا بُدَّأَنْ يَجِيءَ صَاحِبُ هٰذِهِ الْقَاعَةِ فَأَيُّ شَيْءٍ أَقُولُ لَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-yaqūlu lā budda an yajīʾa ṣāḥibu hādhihi al-qāʿati fa-ayyu shayʾin aqūlu lahu
sentences.l: And-he-says: (There is) no escape that comes (the) owner (of) this hall; and-what thing (shall) I-say to-him?
sentences.i: “The master of this hall is bound to come,” he kept saying, “and what shall I tell him?”
sentences.n: lā budda an, 'there is no escape from (the fact) that', 'it must be that'. The print runs budda and an together, بدّان, with the shadda printed; kept as set. yaqūlu, imperfect, 'he says, kept saying'. hādhihi takes a dagger alif. The shadda of ايّ and the ء of شيء and يجيء are printed.

sentences.t: وَلَا بُدَّ أَنَّهُ يَقْتُلُنِي بِلَاشَكٍّ وَتَرُوحُ رُوحِي
sentences.tr: wa-lā budda annahu yaqtulunī bi-lā shakkin wa-tarūḥu rūḥī
sentences.l: And-no escape that-he kills-me without-doubt, and-goes my-soul.
sentences.i: “He is sure to kill me, beyond a doubt, and my life will be gone.”
sentences.n: The print has اله, a misprint for انه, corrected here. lā budda annahu, 'it must be that he …'. bi-lā shakkin, 'without doubt': bi-, 'with', + lā, 'no', together 'without'; printed run together, بلاشكّ, with its shadda; kept as set.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الصَّبِيَّةَ قَامَتْ وَتَشَمَّرَتْ وَأَخَذَتْ خِوَانًا وَقَدْ حَطَّتْ عَلَيْهِ السُّفْرَةَ وَأَكَلَتْ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-ṣabiyyata qāmat wa-tashammarat wa-akhadhat khiwānan wa-qad ḥaṭṭat ʿalayhi al-sufrata wa-akalat
sentences.l: Then indeed the-girl rose and-tucked-up-(her-sleeves) and-took a-table, and-she-had put on-it the-spread, and-she-ate.
sentences.i: Then the girl got up, tucked up her sleeves, took a low table, set out the meal on it, and ate.
sentences.n: tashammarat, Form V of sh-m-r, 'to tuck up one's sleeves or skirts', to set to work; its shadda is printed, as is that of الصبيّة. khiwān, a low dining table or tray-table. ḥaṭṭat, 'she put': ḥaṭṭa, properly 'to set down', is the everyday colloquial verb for 'put'. sufra is the leather or cloth spread for food, and so the meal laid on it.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ لِلْأَمْجَدِ كُلْ يَا سَيِّدِي
sentences.tr: wa-qālat li-al-Amjadi kul yā sayyidī
sentences.l: And-she-said to-al-Amjad: Eat, O my-lord.
sentences.i: “Eat, my lord,” she said to al-Amjad.
sentences.n: kul, 'eat!', the short imperative of akala, which drops its hamza.

sentences.t: فَتَقَدَّمَ الْأَمْجَدُ لِيَأْكُلَ فَمَا طَابَ لَهُ الْأَكْلُ بَلْ صَارَ يَنْظُرُ إِلَى نَاحِيَةِ الْبَابِ حَتَّى أَكَلَتِ الصَّبِيَّةُ وَشَبِعَتْ
sentences.tr: fa-taqaddama al-Amjadu li-yaʾkula fa-mā ṭāba lahu al-aklu bal ṣāra yanẓuru ilā nāḥiyati al-bābi ḥattā akalati al-ṣabiyyatu wa-shabiʿat
sentences.l: And-came-forward al-Amjad to-eat, but-not was-pleasant to-him the-eating; rather he-became looking toward (the) direction (of) the-door, until ate the-girl and-was-sated.
sentences.i: Al-Amjad drew up to eat, but he had no taste for food; he kept looking towards the door, until the girl had eaten her fill.
sentences.n: li-yaʾkula: li- of purpose with the subjunctive, 'in order to eat'. ṭāba lahu, 'it was pleasant to him': li- marks the one it pleases. ṣāra yanẓuru: ṣāra with the imperfect again, 'he took to looking'.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ رَفَعَتِ الْخِوَانَ وَقَدَّمَتْ طَبَقَ الْفَاكِهَةِ وَشَرَعَتْ تَتَنَقَّلُ
sentences.tr: wa-qad rafaʿati al-khiwāna wa-qaddamat ṭabaqa al-fākihati wa-sharaʿat tatanaqqalu
sentences.l: And-she-had lifted the-table and-brought-forward (the) dish (of) the-fruit and-began taking-dessert.
sentences.i: She cleared away the table, brought the dish of fruit, and began to nibble.
sentences.n: tatanaqqalu, Form V of n-q-l, 'to eat naql', the dried fruit, nuts and sweetmeats taken with wine; its shadda is printed. sharaʿa with an imperfect, 'to begin to'.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَدَّمَتِ الْمَشْرُوبَ وَفَتَحَتِ الْجَرَّةَ وَمَلَأَتْ قَدَحًا وَنَاوَلَتْهُ لِلْأَمْجَدِ
sentences.tr: thumma qaddamati al-mashrūba wa-fataḥati al-jarrata wa-malaʾat qadaḥan wa-nāwalathu li-al-Amjadi
sentences.l: Then she-brought-forward the-drink and-opened the-jar and-filled a-cup and-handed-it to-al-Amjad.
sentences.i: Then she brought out the wine, opened the jar, filled a cup and handed it to al-Amjad.
sentences.n: al-mashrūb, 'that which is drunk', here wine. nāwala, Form III, 'to hand'; book Arabic gives it two objects, but here the one handed to is marked with li-, as in later usage. The shadda of الجرّة and the ء of ملأت are printed.

sentences.t: فَأَخَذَهُ مِنْهَا وَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ آهْ آهْ مِنْ صَاحِبِ هٰذِهِ الدَّارِ إِذَا جَاءَ وَرَآنِي
sentences.tr: fa-akhadhahu minhā wa-qāla fī nafsihi āh āh min ṣāḥibi hādhihi al-dāri idhā jāʾa wa-raʾānī
sentences.l: And-he-took-it from-her and-said in himself: Ah, ah, from (the) owner (of) this house when he-comes and-sees-me!
sentences.i: He took it from her and said to himself, “Alas, alas, what the master of this house will do when he comes and sees me!”
sentences.n: āh min, 'ah, from …!', a groan at what someone will do: min names its cause. The madda of آه and of رآني and the ء of جاء are printed. idhā jāʾa wa-raʾānī: perfects after idhā, of the future.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ صَارَتْ عَيْنُهُ صَوْبَ الدِّهْلِيزِ وَالْقَدَحُ فِي يَدِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-qad ṣārat ʿaynuhu ṣawba al-dihlīzi wa-al-qadaḥu fī yadihi
sentences.l: And-had-become his-eye toward the-passage, and-the-cup (was) in his-hand.
sentences.i: His eye was fixed on the entrance passage, the cup in his hand.
sentences.n: ṣawba, 'towards, in the direction of', an adverbial accusative. dihlīz, the vestibule or entrance passage from the street door, is from Persian. wa-al-qadaḥu fī yadihi is a circumstantial clause, 'with the cup in his hand'.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا هُوَ كَذٰلِكَ وَإِذَا بِصَاحِبِ الدَّارِ قَدْ جَاءَ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā huwa ka-dhālika wa-idhā bi-ṣāḥibi al-dāri qad jāʾa
sentences.l: And-while he (was) like-that, and-behold the-owner (of) the-house had come.
sentences.i: While he was in this state, all at once the master of the house arrived.
sentences.n: baynamā … wa-idhā, 'while … , behold': the usual frame for a sudden turn. The bi- after idhā of surprise only marks what appears. ka-dhālika: ka-, 'like', + dhālika, 'that', so 'thus'.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ مَمْلُوكًا مِنْ أَكَابِرِ الْمَدِينَةِ لِأَنَّهُ كَانَ أَمِيرَ يَاخُورٍ عِنْدَ الْمَلِكِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna mamlūkan min akābiri al-madīnati li-annahu kāna amīra yākhūrin ʿinda al-maliki
sentences.l: And-he-was a-mamluk from (the) great-ones (of) the-city, because he was commander (of the) stable with the-king.
sentences.i: He was a mamluk, one of the great men of the city, for he was the king's master of the horse.
sentences.n: mamlūk here in its other sense: a slave-soldier who could rise to the highest offices, as under the Mamluk sultans of Egypt. amīr ākhūr, 'master of the horse', the officer in charge of the royal stables, is a Mamluk title joining Arabic amīr, 'commander', to Persian ākhur, 'stable'. The print spells the second word ياخور, perhaps as it was heard run on from amīr; its vocalisation here as an ordinary genitive, yākhūrin, is a guess. ʿinda al-malik, 'with the king', in his service.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ جَعَلَ تِلْكَ الْقَاعَةَ مُعَدَّةً لِحَظِّهِ لِيَنْشَرِحَ فِيهَا صَدْرُهُ وَيَخْتَلِيَ فِيهَا بِمَنْ يُرِيدُهُ
sentences.tr: wa-qad jaʿala tilka al-qāʿata muʿaddatan li-ḥaẓẓihi li-yanshariḥa fīhā ṣadruhu wa-yakhtaliya fīhā bi-man yurīduhu
sentences.l: And-he-had made that hall prepared for-his-pleasure, that might-expand in-it his-breast and-he-might-be-alone in-it with-whom he-wants-him.
sentences.i: He had fitted out that hall for his pleasure, a place where he could take his ease and be alone with whomever he wished.
sentences.n: muʿadda, 'made ready'; its shadda is printed. li-ḥaẓẓihi: li-, 'for', + ḥaẓẓ, properly 'lot, fortune', in later usage 'pleasure, enjoyment'; the shadda of لحظّه is printed. li-yanshariḥa: li- of purpose with the subjunctive; inshirāḥ al-ṣadr, 'the broadening of the breast', is ease and delight. ikhtalā bi-, 'to be alone with': bi- marks the companion. yurīduhu, 'whom he wants', with the returning pronoun -hu.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ فِي ذٰلِكَ الْيَوْمِ قَدْ أَرْسَلَ إِلَى مَعْشُوقٍ يَجِيءُ لَهُ وَقَدْ جَهَّزَ لَهُ ذٰلِكَ الْمَكَانَ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna fī dhālika al-yawmi qad arsala ilā maʿshūqin yajīʾu lahu wa-qad jahhaza lahu dhālika al-makāna
sentences.l: And-he-had on that day sent to a-beloved (that) he-come to-him, and-he-had prepared for-him that place.
sentences.i: That very day he had sent for a lover of his to come to him, and had made the place ready for him.
sentences.n: kāna … qad arsala, 'he had sent', a pluperfect. maʿshūq, 'one passionately loved', is masculine; love language often uses the masculine of a woman too, so the grammar alone does not settle who the beloved is, though nothing here points to a woman. arsala ilā, 'to send to (someone)', here 'to send for'. yajīʾu lahu, 'he comes to him', is a bare imperfect clause of purpose, without an; the ء of يجيء is printed. In jahhaza lahu, li- is 'for him', the beloved. The shadda of جهّز is printed.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ اسْمُ ذٰلِكَ الْمَمْلُوكِ بَهَادُرَ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna ismu dhālika al-mamlūki Bahādura
sentences.l: And-was (the) name (of) that mamluk Bahādur.
sentences.i: The name of this mamluk was Bahādur.
sentences.n: Bahādur, 'valiant, hero', a Turco-Persian title that became a common name among the Mamluks; as a foreign name it is treated as a diptote, Bahādura.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ سَخِيَّ الْيَدِ صَاحِبَ جُودٍ وَإِحْسَانٍ وَصَدَقَاتٍ وَامْتِنَانٍ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna sakhiyya al-yadi ṣāḥiba jūdin wa-iḥsānin wa-ṣadaqātin wa-imtinānin
sentences.l: And-he-was generous (of) the-hand, possessor (of) liberality and-beneficence and-alms and-favours.
sentences.i: He was open-handed, a man of generosity and kindness, of alms and bounty.
sentences.n: sakhiyy al-yad, 'generous of hand'; the shadda of سخيّ is printed. ṣāḥib, 'possessor of', builds an epithet. imtinān is here the bestowing of favours. The sajʿ falls on iḥsān / imtinān.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا وَصَلَ إِلَى قَرِيبٍ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā waṣala ilā qarībin
sentences.l: And-when he-arrived to near …
sentences.i: When he drew near …
sentences.n: The night breaks off in mid-sentence: ilā qarīb, 'to (a place) near', and the sentence goes on in the next night.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. The rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥ / al-mubāḥ. The print splits the name across a line-end here, شهر / زاد; it is kept as two words.
